slides.title: Learning Objective
slides.text:
Learning Objective

•  By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:
   – Understand spatial representation as the combination of position and
       orientation.
   – Recognize the importance of the rotation matrix and explain its
      fundamental properties.
   – Differentiate between fixed-angle (extrinsic) and Euler-angle (intrinsic)
       representations of orientation.

slides.title: Introduction
slides.text:
Introduction

•  Robotic manipulation, by definition, implies that parts and tools will be
  moved around in space by some sort of mechanism.
•  Robotic manipulators operate in three-dimensional space and consist of
   rigid links connected by joints.
•  In order to analyze, model, and control these systems, a precise
   mathematical description of position, orientation, and spatial
   relationships is required.
• We assume that somewhere there is a universe coordinate system to
   which everything can be referenced.
• We describe all positions and orientations with
   respect to the universe coordinate system or with
   respect to other Cartesian coordinate systems that
   are defined relative to the universe system.


                                                                                                           4

slides.title: Spatial Representation of Rigid Bodies
slides.text:
Spatial Representation of Rigid Bodies
•  Coordinate Frames
   – Frame, is a set of four vectors giving position and
       orientation information.
   – A coordinate frame is defined by an origin and three
       mutually orthogonal unit vectors ො𝐱,ො𝐲, ො𝐳.
   –  In robotics, coordinate frames are rigidly attached to
       robot links in order to describe their motion and
       geometry.
   – Common frames include:
           • Base frame (fixed to the robot base)
           • Link frames (attached to each link)
           • End-effector frame (attached to the tool or gripper)
           • Goal Frame Location where the robot is desired
            to move.


                                                                                                           5

slides.title: Spatial Representation of Rigid Bodies (Cont.)
slides.text:
Spatial Representation of Rigid Bodies (Cont.)

•  Position Vectors
    – Once a coordinate system is established, we can locate any point in the universe
       with a 3 x 1 position vector.
    – Each of these distances along an axis can be thought of as the result of projecting
       the vector onto the corresponding axis.
    – We will describe the position of a point in space with a position vector.
    – The position of a point 𝑃 relative to a coordinate frame {A} is represented by a
        vector:
                          𝑝𝑥
   𝐀𝐏= 𝑝𝑥෡𝑿𝑨+𝑝𝑌෡𝒀𝑨+𝑝𝑍෡𝒁𝑨= 𝑝𝑦
                            𝑝𝑧



                                                                                                           6

visualInspection.notes: Viewed the faithful full 1800x1013 page image at original detail alongside extracted text. Footer read from pixels. Raster equations/code, signs, axis labels, matrix products and diagrams inspected. A position vector is a 3x1 vector of projections along reference axes: ^A P = p_x X_A + p_y Y_A + p_z Z_A = [p_x,p_y,p_z]^T. The arrow runs from the origin of frame A to point P.

slides.title: Spatial Representation of Rigid Bodies (Cont.)
slides.text:
Spatial Representation of Rigid Bodies (Cont.)

•  Orientation Representation
    –  To describe an object in space, we need to specify its
        position as well as its orientation.
    – While position describes where an object or manipulation
           is located, orientation describes how it is rotated relative to
       another coordinate frame.
    – Assuming that the manipulator has sufficient number of
         joints to orient the object in desired orientation while
       keeping the fingertip at same position in space.
    –  To describe the orientation of a body, we attach a
       coordinate system to the body and then give a description
        of this coordinate system relative to the reference system.
    – One way to describe the body attached coordinate system
        {B} is to write the unit vectors of its three principal axes in
       terms of the coordinate system {A}.



                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Viewed the faithful full 1800x1013 page image at original detail alongside extracted text. Footer read from pixels. Raster equations/code, signs, axis labels, matrix products and diagrams inspected. Complete body description needs position and orientation. With enough joints the fingertip position can remain fixed while orientation changes. Attach frame B to the body and describe its unit vectors relative to frame A.

slides.title: – We denote the unit vectors giving the principal directions of coordinate
slides.text:
– We denote the unit vectors giving the principal directions of coordinate
  system {B} as ෡𝑿𝑩, ෡𝒀𝑩,and ෡𝒁𝑩.
– When written in terms of coordinate system {A}, they are
   called 𝑨෡𝑿𝑩, 𝑨෡𝒀𝑩, and 𝑨෡𝒁𝑩
–  It will be convenient if we stack these three unit vectors
   together as the columns of a 3 x 3 matrix, in the order 𝑨෡𝑿𝑩,
    𝑨෡𝒀𝑩, 𝑨෡𝒁𝑩.
– We will call this matrix a Rotation matrix

slides.title: Rotation Matrices
slides.text:
Rotation Matrices
•  Definition
   – A rotation matrix 𝑩𝑨𝐑 expresses the orientation of frame {B} relative to
      frame {A}.
   –  It is a 3×3 matrix whose columns correspond to the unit vectors of frame {B}
      expressed in frame {A}:
                                     𝑟11   𝑟12   𝑟13
     𝑨𝐑=                  =  𝑟21   𝑟22   𝑟23      𝑩    𝑨෡𝑿𝑩   𝑨෡𝒀𝑩   𝑨෡𝒁𝑩
                                     𝑟31   𝑟32   𝑟33
      So position is represented by a vector while
        orientation is represented by a matrix.




                                                                                                           9

Raster equations/code, signs, axis labels, matrix products and diagrams inspected. ^A_B R = [^A X_B, ^A Y_B, ^A Z_B] = [[r11,r12,r13],[r21,r22,r23],[r31,r32,r33]].

•  Component of any vector are the projection of vector into unit directions of the
   reference frame.
•  Dot product of unit vectors are cosine of angles between them so components
   of the rotation matrix are often referred as direction cosines.
•  Properties of Rotation Matrices
   –  Orthogonality: 𝐑𝐓𝐑 = 𝐑𝐑𝐓= I
   – Determinant: det(𝑅)=1
   –  Inverse equals transpose: 𝐑−𝟏=𝐑𝐓

slides.title: Mapping from Frame to Frame
slides.text:
Mapping from Frame to Frame

•  Mapping: Changing description from frame to frame
•   Translational mapping
    –  In this case, {B} differs from {A} only by a
        translation({A} and {B} are in same orientation), which is
       given by 𝐀𝐏𝐁𝐎𝐑𝐆, a vector
        that locates the origin of {B} relative to {A}.
    – 𝐀𝐏= 𝐁𝐏+ 𝐀𝐏𝐁𝐎𝐑𝐆

  •  Rotational mapping
       In this case, {B} differs from {A} only
      by an orientation with their origins
                         𝐀𝐑 a 3x3       coinciding, which is given by,𝐁
       rotation matrix.
         𝐀𝐏= 𝐀𝐑 𝐁𝐏                  𝐁


                                                                                                          16

slides.title: Rotation Matrices (Cont.)
slides.text:
Rotation Matrices (Cont.)

•   In robotic systems and rigid body kinematics, describing the spatial configuration of a
   body requires specifying both its position and orientation.
•  While position can be represented using a three-dimensional vector, orientation is
    inherently more complex. It raises important questions:
    –  About which axes should rotations be performed?
    –  In what order should these rotations occur?
    –  Should the rotations be about fixed reference axes or about moving body axes?
•  A fundamental result from rigid body kinematics states that any arbitrary orientation in
   three-dimensional space can be achieved through three
    successive rotations about coordinate axes.
•  The interpretation of these rotations leads to 2 principal
    representations:
    –  Fixed-angle rotations and Euler-angle rotations


                                                                                                          23

visualInspection.notes: Viewed the faithful full 1800x1013 page image at original detail alongside extracted text. Footer read from pixels. Raster equations/code, signs, axis labels, matrix products and diagrams inspected. Pose consists of position and orientation. Three successive rotations about coordinate axes can describe arbitrary orientation. The axes, their order, and whether axes are fixed or moving must be specified. Fixed-angle and Euler-angle representations are introduced.

               •   Finally about ෡𝒁𝐴 by an angle α

slides.title: Rotation Matrices (Cont.)
slides.text:
Rotation Matrices (Cont.)

•  An extrinsic X–Y–Z rotation is mathematically equivalent to an intrinsic
  Z–Y–X rotation.
•  This equivalence arises because:
   – Matrix multiplication order determines the frame with respect to which
        rotations are applied
   – Changing from fixed axes to moving axes reverses the physical rotation
      sequence
•  In Rotation matrix, among the nine equations are six dependencies, so,
   essentially, we have three equations and three unknowns
   –  Pitch angle β = Atan2(−𝑟31,  𝑟112+𝑟212 )
   – Yaw angle α = Atan2(𝑟21/𝑐β, 𝑟11/𝑐β)
   –  Roll angle ϒ = Atan2(𝑟32/𝑐β, 𝑟33/𝑐β)
   – These formulas assume cosβ≠0.


                                                                                                          28

visualInspection.notes: Viewed the faithful full 1800x1013 page image at original detail alongside extracted text. Footer read from pixels. Raster equations/code, signs, axis labels, matrix products and diagrams inspected. Extrinsic X-Y-Z is mathematically equivalent to intrinsic Z-Y-X; changing fixed to moving axes reverses the physical sequence. A rotation matrix has nine entries and six dependencies. beta=Atan2(-r31,sqrt(r11^2+r21^2)); alpha=Atan2(r21/cos(beta),r11/cos(beta)); gamma=Atan2(r32/cos(beta),r33/cos(beta)). These formulas assume cos(beta) != 0.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•  A robotic manipulator consists of rigid links connected by joints forming a
   kinematic chain
•  Links maintain fixed geometric relationships between joint axes
•   Joints constrain relative motion; most manipulators use revolute or prismatic
    joints
•  Links are numbered from the fixed base (link 0) to the end-effector (link n)
•  Coordinate frames are attached to each link to describe position and
   orientation
•  Position is represented using vectors; orientation is
   represented using rotation matrices
•  Homogeneous transformation matrices combine rotation
   and translation into a single representation


                                                                                                          29

Coordinate frames attach to links; position uses vectors, orientation rotation matrices, and homogeneous transformations combine rotation and translation.

sourceIssues.finding: The lecture title names DH parameters, but pages 212–242 develop spatial representations, not a DH parameter table or the four-parameter DH transform.
sourceIssues.handling: Do not invent DH questions for this lecture merely from the title; detailed DH content needs its later actual source.

sourceIssues.finding: The caption says apply another y-axis rotation without declaring fixed or moving axes; code is explicitly Rx(pi/2) @ Ry(pi/2).
sourceIssues.handling: Questions state the exact product and column/frame convention; the body-axis interpretation is supported by later intrinsic-axis derivation.

sourceIssues.finding: Compact ^A P=T ^B P notation precedes the 4x4 homogeneous matrix without visibly appending 1 to each Cartesian point symbol.
sourceIssues.handling: Questions distinguish the 3-vector affine equation from homogeneous [p;1] multiplication; no 4x4-by-3x1 product is accepted.

sourceIssues.finding: The displayed pure-Z formula is homogeneous 4x4, while the animation calls rotz(t), associated with 3x3 rotations on the earlier slide.
sourceIssues.handling: Record both representations honestly; do not claim the code explicitly constructs 4x4 matrices or that visualization-library execution was tested.

sourceIssues.finding: The displayed numerical rotation uses cos30=0.866, so its literal rounded columns are not exactly unit length.
sourceIssues.handling: Use exact trig for symbolic properties and explicitly state final rounding; the worked output is reproduced to three decimals.

sourceIssues.finding: The first comment says local X but calls rotz(alpha); the final comment says local Z but calls rotx(gamma). The calls, title, adjacent derivation, and printed output agree on intrinsic Z-Y-X.
sourceIssues.handling: Flag comments as swapped. One question explicitly asks for the comment correction; other questions follow executable calls and state their sequence.

sourceIssues.finding: The inverse formulas assume cos(beta)!=0; the positive square root selects a principal pitch branch and does not imply global uniqueness of angle triples.
sourceIssues.handling: Questions preserve the nonsingularity hypothesis, specify Atan2 convention when needed, and distinguish parametrization singularity from matrix singularity.
